title: Forms of Stratification
description: Caste, estate, and class — the architecture of social inequality

concepts.title: What Stratification Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Social stratification is the structured ranking of groups in a society into hierarchical layers, with unequal access to rewards: wealth, power, prestige, and life chances. Crucially, it is not merely individual variation — it is patterned, persistent, and reproduced across generations.

Sociologists distinguish stratification systems by how positions are allocated. Ascribed statuses are assigned at birth (caste, hereditary nobility, race in many societies); achieved statuses are earned through effort or competition (occupation, credentials, wealth in modern markets).

No real society is purely one or the other. Modern liberal democracies promise achievement-based mobility but in practice show heavy ascriptive inheritance: children of high-income parents disproportionately become high-income adults. The gap between ideology and reality is itself a central object of study — what Michael Young in 1958 satirically called the 'meritocracy.'

concepts.title: Caste, Estate, Class
concepts.contentHtml:
Three classical types of stratification system have shaped sociological theory.

Caste systems (most famously in South Asia) are closed: membership is hereditary, endogamy is enforced, and ritual purity governs interaction. Movement between castes is essentially impossible within a lifetime.

Estate systems (medieval Europe) divided society into legally defined orders — clergy, nobility, commoners — each with distinct rights and obligations under law. Mobility was rare but not absolutely barred; the orders were political-legal categories enforced by the state.

Class systems (industrial and post-industrial societies) are formally open: legal equality prevails, mobility is possible, and class position depends on market position rather than birth status. But class systems still produce massive inequality and substantial inheritance of position. Class is economic rather than legal — and that change is what Marx and Weber set out to theorise.

concepts.title: Life Chances and Inequality
concepts.contentHtml:
Max Weber introduced the term life chances (Lebenschancen) to describe the probabilities, given your structural position, of obtaining things people want and avoiding things people fear: health, education, security, satisfying work, long life.

Stratification matters because it distributes life chances unequally. In the United Kingdom, men in the most deprived areas can expect roughly a decade fewer years of life than men in the wealthiest. Children born into the bottom income quintile are much less likely to attend selective universities, regardless of measured ability.

Inequality of outcome (income, wealth) and inequality of opportunity (the chance to acquire those outcomes) are conceptually distinct. Many political disputes turn on which kind matters. Sociology shows they are tightly entangled in practice: parental outcomes shape children's opportunities through schooling, networks, neighbourhoods, and culture.

title: Theories of Class
description: Marx, Weber, and the modern class schemes

concepts.title: Marx: Bourgeoisie and Proletariat
concepts.contentHtml:
For Karl Marx, class is defined by relation to the means of production. Under capitalism, two principal classes confront each other: the bourgeoisie, who own productive capital, and the proletariat, who own only their labour-power and must sell it to live.

The relationship is not merely unequal but exploitative: workers produce value beyond what they receive in wages, and this surplus value is appropriated by capital. Class conflict is structural, not a misunderstanding to be resolved by goodwill.

Marx distinguished a class in itself (sharing objective economic position) from a class for itself (conscious of shared interests and organised to pursue them). Capitalism, he predicted, would tend to polarise society and generate the proletarian class consciousness needed for revolutionary change. The 20th century complicated this picture, but the idea that economic ownership structures social power remains influential.

concepts.title: Weber's Three Dimensions
concepts.contentHtml:
Max Weber accepted that economic position matters but argued Marx's two-class model was too narrow. Stratification, Weber held, has three analytically distinct dimensions: class, status, and party.

Class refers to one's market position — what you can offer in the labour and capital markets. Weber subdivided this finely (skilled and unskilled labour, professionals, propertied groups) rather than collapsing everything into two camps.

Status (Stand) refers to social honour or prestige — lifestyle, consumption patterns, networks of recognition. Status groups can cut across classes (think of impoverished aristocrats or wealthy outsiders denied prestige).

Party refers to organised power — political parties, unions, professional associations. The three dimensions correlate but can come apart, and treating them as independent allowed Weber to analyse phenomena, like ethnic stratification, that pure economism misses.

concepts.title: Modern Class Schemes: Wright and Goldthorpe
concepts.contentHtml:
Twentieth-century sociologists translated Marx and Weber into operational class schemes for survey research.

Erik Olin Wright's neo-Marxist scheme kept ownership of the means of production central but added contradictory class locations for managers and professionals — wage-earners who nonetheless exercise authority and possess scarce skills. Wright's mature scheme cross-classified people by ownership, authority, and skill assets.

John Goldthorpe's EGP scheme (Erikson–Goldthorpe–Portocarero), broadly Weberian, classifies people by employment relations: service relationships (salaried professionals and managers, with autonomy, career structure, and prospects), labour contracts (manual and routine workers, paid for discrete effort), and intermediate forms. EGP underlies the UK's official NS-SEC classification and most European mobility research. Both schemes show that class still strongly predicts health, voting, and life chances even in 'post-industrial' economies.

title: Functionalism and Its Critics
description: Davis and Moore, Tumin, and the debate over whether inequality is necessary

concepts.title: Davis and Moore: Stratification as Functional
concepts.contentHtml:
In a famous 1945 paper, Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore offered a functionalist defence of social inequality. Every society, they argued, must motivate its most talented members to undertake its most important and demanding positions — surgeon, judge, engineer.

This requires differential rewards: higher pay, prestige, and authority attached to more functionally important and harder-to-fill roles. Inequality, on this view, is not an unfortunate accident but a functional necessity for any complex society.

Davis and Moore were careful to distinguish position-based rewards from inheritance: their argument justifies unequal positions, not unequal starting points. They were describing a logic of social organisation, not endorsing existing distributions of wealth.

Their account fits a broader functionalist program (Parsons, Merton) that asks what each social institution contributes to system stability. It became the orthodox American account of stratification through the 1950s.

concepts.title: The Tumin Critique
concepts.contentHtml:
Melvin Tumin's 1953 reply, 'Some Principles of Stratification: A Critical Analysis', is the canonical critique of Davis and Moore.

Tumin pressed several points. First, functional importance is hard to measure: we cannot run the experiment of removing surgeons or removing sanitation workers to see which the society misses more. Second, the supply of talent is not naturally scarce — much potential talent never gets developed because access to education and opportunity is itself unequal.

Third, large rewards are not always needed for motivation: many vital roles (parents, teachers, nurses) are filled by people for modest pay. Fourth, inheritance, networks, and discrimination all interfere with the meritocratic matching the theory presupposes. Fifth, stratification has dysfunctions: wasted talent, social conflict, weakened solidarity, ideological distortion.

Tumin's critique didn't kill functionalist accounts entirely, but it opened space for conflict-theoretic alternatives that took inequality and power, not consensus, as the starting point.

concepts.title: Conflict Theory and Power
concepts.contentHtml:
Conflict theorists, drawing on Marx and Weber, view stratification as the outcome of power struggles rather than functional necessity. Groups with resources defend and extend their advantages; subordinate groups resist or are excluded.

Ralf Dahrendorf reframed class as relations of authority rather than property: the line between command and obedience generates conflict in any organised setting, not only capitalist enterprise. This widened the analysis of stratification beyond ownership of capital.

Frank Parkin developed the Weberian idea of social closure: dominant groups protect their position through exclusion (formal credentials, professional licensing, restrictive networks), while subordinate groups respond through usurpation (collective action, unions, political mobilisation). Closure analysis explains how seemingly meritocratic devices — degree requirements, professional bodies — can function as inheritance mechanisms in disguise. Charles Tilly's later 'opportunity hoarding' is a direct descendant.

title: Measuring Inequality and Mobility
description: Income, wealth, the Gini coefficient, Piketty, and how mobility is measured

concepts.title: Income, Wealth, and the Gini Coefficient
concepts.contentHtml:
Income and wealth are not the same. Income is a flow — what you earn or receive in a year. Wealth is a stock — the assets you own minus debts. Wealth is typically far more unequally distributed than income, because it accumulates over a lifetime and is inherited across generations.

The Gini coefficient is the standard summary measure: 0 means perfect equality (everyone has the same), 1 means perfect inequality (one person has everything). Most developed countries have income Ginis between 0.25 (Nordic countries, post-tax) and 0.40 (United States). Wealth Ginis are much higher — typically 0.65 to 0.85.

The Gini compresses distributional information into a single number, so two very different distributions can share a Gini. Sociologists supplement it with top-share measures: the share of income or wealth held by the top 1% or 10%. These measures, popularised by Anthony Atkinson and Thomas Piketty, capture concentration at the top that the Gini can blur.

concepts.title: Piketty: r > g
concepts.contentHtml:
Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014) marshalled centuries of tax records to track wealth concentration in the long run. His central claim is summarised in an inequality: r > g.

Here r is the average rate of return on capital and g is the rate of economic growth. When returns on capital persistently exceed growth, existing wealth grows faster than the overall economy, so accumulated and inherited fortunes increase as a share of total wealth. The result is a long-run drift toward the dominance of inheritance over earned income.

Piketty argued the relatively equal mid-20th century in Europe and the US was a historical exception, produced by the destruction of capital in two world wars and high taxation, not by a built-in tendency of capitalism. Since 1980, inequality has climbed sharply in many wealthy countries, especially the US and UK. His policy proposals — including a global wealth tax — generated as much debate as the empirics.

concepts.title: Social Mobility: Types and Measures
concepts.contentHtml:
Mobility research distinguishes several axes. Intergenerational mobility compares parents and children; intragenerational mobility tracks an individual across their own working life. Absolute mobility asks whether people are better off than their parents in level terms (often driven by economic growth); relative mobility asks about positional change — whether the child of a low-ranked parent is likely to overtake the child of a high-ranked parent.

The Great Gatsby curve, named by Alan Krueger and built on Miles Corak's data, plots cross-country inequality against intergenerational income elasticity. More unequal societies (US, UK) tend to have less mobility; more equal ones (Denmark, Canada) have more.

Raj Chetty and colleagues used US tax records to map mobility by neighbourhood, finding striking geographic variation: the chance a child born poor reaches the top quintile differs sharply between cities and even between adjacent zip codes. Place, networks, schools, and family structure all leave fingerprints in the data.

title: Reproduction, Poverty, and Global Inequality
description: Bourdieu, Lareau, the underclass debate, and inequality between nations

concepts.title: Bourdieu and Cultural Reproduction
concepts.contentHtml:
Pierre Bourdieu argued that inequality is reproduced not only through money but through cultural capital: dispositions, tastes, manners, and forms of knowledge that schools and elite institutions implicitly reward.

Middle-class children arrive at school already speaking the school's language — used to formal vocabulary, abstract reasoning, museum visits, classical music. Their habitus — the durable set of dispositions instilled by their upbringing — fits the institution. Working-class children, equally bright, must adapt to a code their family did not transmit.

Schools then certify these inherited differences as 'merit', laundering background advantage into qualifications. Bourdieu also identified social capital (network ties) and symbolic capital (legitimised prestige). Cultural reproduction explains why educational expansion has not closed mobility gaps as much as functionalist accounts predicted: when everyone has a degree, what matters is which degree, from which institution, with which connections.

concepts.title: Lareau, Tracking, and Opportunity Hoarding
concepts.contentHtml:
Annette Lareau's ethnography Unequal Childhoods (2003) followed American families across class lines. She found two distinct child-rearing logics. Middle-class parents practised concerted cultivation: scheduled activities, deliberate vocabulary development, training children to negotiate with adults and institutions. Working-class and poor families practised the accomplishment of natural growth: more unstructured time, clearer authority lines, less institutional engagement.

Both produce competent children, but only one produces the skills schools and employers reward. The mechanism converts class into life chances even when parental warmth and aspiration are equal.

Within schools, tracking (streaming) reinforces these gaps: assignment to higher tracks correlates with class background and shapes future opportunities. Charles Tilly's opportunity hoarding generalises the pattern: advantaged groups corner access to valuable resources — good schools, internships, professional networks — and pass that access to insiders. Categorical inequality persists because gates are kept, not because talent is lacking.

concepts.title: Poverty and Global Inequality
concepts.contentHtml:
Absolute poverty is defined by inability to meet basic needs (food, shelter, health). Relative poverty, championed by Peter Townsend, defines deprivation in terms of the standards of one's own society — being unable to participate in customary life, even if calorie intake is adequate. Most developed countries officially measure relative poverty (e.g. below 60% of median income).

William Julius Wilson's The Truly Disadvantaged (1987) reframed the American 'underclass' debate. Wilson argued that concentrated urban poverty was driven not by a culture of dependency but by structural shifts: deindustrialisation, the disappearance of stable working-class jobs, and the residential segregation that concentrated joblessness in inner cities.

At the global scale, world-system theory (Immanuel Wallerstein) divides nations into core, semi-periphery, and periphery, with unequal exchange transferring value upward. The Kuznets curve hypothesised an inverted-U: inequality rises and then falls as countries industrialise. Recent decades, with rising within-country inequality across the rich world, have cast the simple Kuznets story into doubt — though global between-country inequality has fallen as Asia has grown.
